title: Indian American Candidates Split Final Pitches Between Local Issues and Trump
excerpt: On the eve of the midterms, Republicans Ramaswamy and Komatireddy closed on crime, taxes and energy costs, while Democrats Subramanyam, Khanna and Sethi framed the vote as a check on Trump and a stand against anti-Indian hate.
body:
• Republican Indian American candidates closed on crime, property taxes and living costs, while Democrats cast Tuesday's vote as a check on President Donald Trump.
  • Ohio governor nominee Vivek Ramaswamy ended his statewide swing in Cleveland promising to slash property taxes, restore law on the streets and cut electric bills by producing more energy.
  • Virginia Congressman Suhas Subramanyam framed the election as choosing "a Congress that works for the people, not the President"; Texas candidate Pooja Sethi closed against anti-Indian hate.
  • These races are decided on Tuesday, November 3 — Ramaswamy's Ohio governorship bid and Saritha Komatireddy's challenge for New York attorney general are among the results the community will watch first.

Indian American candidates made sharply different closing arguments on the eve of Tuesday's US midterm elections, according to IANS reporting carried by New India Abroad. Republicans pressed crime and living costs. Democrats cast the vote as a check on President Donald Trump and a stand against rising hate. The contrast was not about whether to mention the community's story — both sides did — but about what the final day of campaigning should be about: the price of living in a state, or the direction of the country.

The Republican pitch: taxes, crime and energy

In Ohio, Republican governor nominee Vivek Ramaswamy ended a statewide swing in Cleveland. His closing post on X was a list of state-level promises, not a national argument.

"Slash property taxes quickly. Restore the rule of law on our streets. Cut electric bills by producing more energy. This isn't right vs. left. It's right vs. wrong. It's common sense vs. crazy. That's the choice tomorrow."

— Vivek Ramaswamy, Republican nominee for Ohio governor

After a stop in Toledo, Ramaswamy added a state-first line: "Ohioans first, that's my sole responsibility as Governor." The framing deliberately kept the race local — property taxes, street safety and electricity bills are levers a governor can plausibly pull, and his pitch asked voters to judge the contest on those terms rather than as a referendum on Washington.

In New York, Republican Saritha Komatireddy, who is challenging Attorney General Letitia James, toured Buffalo, Rochester, Syracuse and Binghamton before a last stop on Long Island. "Crime, homelessness and fraud are all up under Letitia James, and she wouldn't change a thing. I'm the change New Yorkers have been waiting for," she posted. Komatireddy, the daughter of Indian immigrants, also tied her pitch to the immigrant story. Her campaign quoted her as saying: "You come to this country because there's a promise and a hope that if you work hard … you can provide for yourself and your family."

The Democratic pitch: Trump, Iran and hate

On the Democratic side, the closing arguments ran through the president. Congressman Suhas Subramanyam of Virginia framed the election directly around Trump: "Tomorrow we will elect a Congress that works for the people, not the President," he posted.

Congressman Ro Khanna of California used the final weekend to push his Iran message. "Dems can vote to zero out appropriations for the war in Iran," he wrote, adding that Trump had called him "a lightweight 4 times." Where Subramanyam offered a constitutional argument — Congress as a check — Khanna offered a policy one: use Congress's power over spending to end funding for the war.

In Texas, Pooja Sethi, the Democratic candidate for state House District 47, closed on the anti-Indian hate that has shadowed the state's campaign. "We will not be intimidated. We will not be silenced. Hate has no home in Texas," she wrote. Her closing message treated the hate directed at South Asian communities during the campaign as itself an election issue, not background noise.

In Florida, Democrat Pia Dandiya, whose race in the 22nd Congressional District has drawn heavy outside spending, posted: "We have 1 day left to fight for a future worthy of our children."

What the split shows

The split mirrors the national campaign, in which Republicans have stressed crime and prices while Democrats have focused on Trump, the Iran war and affordability, the IANS report said. What is new is that the mirror now runs through one community's candidates on both sides. Indian American contenders are no longer clustered in one party's message; a Republican is making the cost-of-living case in Ohio while a Democrat makes the anti-hate case in Texas.

For diaspora voters, the practical point is that there is no single "Indian American pitch" to evaluate this year. A voter in Ohio is being asked about property taxes and electric bills; a voter in Virginia is being asked whether Congress should check the president; a voter in Texas District 47 is being asked how their representative responds to hate against their own community. The answers arrive on Tuesday, when polls decide all of these races.
